papers.title: Suppressing Chaos Without Silencing Excitable Oscillators
papers.abstract: A negative Lyapunov exponent is not a sufficient goal for controlling an excitable oscillator. A gain can remove chaos by removing the excitation that the model is meant to keep. This manuscript studies that failure mode in three models: the forced FitzHugh--Nagumo neuron, the forced Aliev--Panfilov cardiac cell, and the autonomous Hindmarsh--Rose neuron. Chaos is measured by the largest state Lyapunov exponent. Excitation is measured by threshold crossings, by the excursion of the fast variable, and by the firing rate. Recovery damping, tracking of an unstable periodic orbit, Pyragas delayed feedback, and a change of the fast time scale are compared on the same chaotic regimes. In the forced models, large damping and large rate changes reach regularity by silencing the cell, while tracking and delayed feedback keep firing. In the autonomous model, recovery damping raises the firing rate several-fold instead. A classical matrix-measure bound links these outcomes to the channel through which the gain acts. A constant-metric contraction certificate coexists with substantial firing only under tracking, which subtracts a gain from the fast direction.

papers.title: The Thue-Morse route to chaos in the open quantum baker map
papers.abstract: We study the resonances of the quantum baker map opened by a window of width $w$ centred at $q_c$. For $q_c=1/2$ the survivor set of the classical doubling map with a hole goes from zero to positive topological entropy along the Thue-Morse route, and we find numerically, for $N$ up to $2^{25}$, that the resonance spectrum follows this route step by step, also where the entropy is zero. Below the threshold $w_c=4a^*-1$, with $a^*$ the Thue-Morse constant, the surviving cycles have periods $2^\nu$ and their thresholds accumulate doubly exponentially. Each cycle gives, as isolated orbits do, a multiplet of resonances close to modulus $2^{-1/2}$, with phases set by its action. Since a cycle is resolved only if its period is shorter than about $\log_2 N$, twice the Ehrenfest time, about $\log_2\log_2 N$ steps are resolved, four at our largest sizes. Near $w_c$ the 16-cycle perturbs the 8-multiplet through a return path that classically opens only at $w_c$. Cutting a few sites of this path removes the perturbation. At $w_c$ the leading resonance jumps within one or two lattice sites, since a window one site wider than the threshold already has an entropy of order $1/\log_2 N$. One site or more above $w_c$ it lies between 0.93 and 1.00 times the value set by the topological pressure, with no free parameter. There the Walsh eigenvalue count grows with the fractal Weyl exponent, and the Fourier count with an exponent a few hundredths smaller at the sizes we reach.

papers.title: Trajectory arclength reveals thermodynamic criticality
papers.abstract: Thermodynamic criticality arises at continuous phase transitions, where collective interactions produce non-analytic behavior in equilibrium thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit. We show that this criticality also leaves an analytically predictable signature in the arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories. For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, we derive the thermodynamic limit of the equilibrium-averaged arclength, formulated as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, and demonstrate that it develops a kink precisely at the phase transition. We trace this non-analyticity to spontaneous magnetization and derive the leading critical finite-size correction, scaling as $N^{-1/2}$ with an explicit analytical prefactor. Simulations with up to $10^5$ degrees of freedom confirm both predictions without adjustable parameters. Requiring neither tangent-space evolution nor prior specification of an order parameter for its computation, trajectory arclength provides a simple, quantitative link between microscopic Hamiltonian motion and collective thermodynamic criticality.

papers.title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
papers.abstract: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.

papers.title: Construction of a Deployable Closure Model for the Transport of Turbulence Dissipation Rate with Hard-Constrained Physics-Informed Machine Learning
papers.abstract: We present a hard-constrained physics-informed machine learning (PIML) method for constructing a deployable closure model for the transport of turbulence dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals. This coupling allows us to learn the closure without using reference closure values as training targets. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We study decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) and learn $\psi$, the closure function governing dissipation rate decay, from trajectories obtained in experiments and direct numerical simulations. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. The framework reduces the root mean square of the closure variation across ten random seeds by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number $Re_{\lambda_g}$ and can be exported as a standalone C function.

papers.title: Stable eigenmodes of the Large-scale circulation in Turbulent Convection
papers.abstract: Turbulent Rayleigh-B\'enard convection (RBC) is a canonical system for studying buoyancy-driven turbulence. Its defining feature is a system-size large-scale circulation (LSC), whose dynamics reflect the coupling between coherent motion and turbulent fluctuations. Starting from the Boussinesq Navier-Stokes and temperature equations, we derive three coupled stochastic equations for the LSC angular velocity and its associated dipolar temperature field. The deterministic dynamics contain an unstable no-LSC set and two symmetry-related stable finite-LSC states. Linearization about either finite-LSC state yields one purely relaxational eigenmode and a pair of damped oscillatory eigenmodes whose frequency is set by the LSC turnover rate. Turbulent fluctuations continually excite the latter, providing a dynamical origin for the observed quasi-periodic oscillations. Experiments in a thin-disk cell directly resolve both eigenmodes and show their predicted Rayleigh-number scalings. The same stochastic dynamics also provide a route to rare cessations and reversals. This theory-experiment framework provides a tractable example of how coherent circulation states, intrinsic modes, and fluctuation-driven transitions emerge in turbulent convection, with broader relevance to geophysical and astrophysical flows.

papers.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
papers.abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.

papers.title: Fractal dimension of velocity-driven mixing: Reanalysis of Cao et al. (Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)) and the universality of the Marstrand co-dimension rule
papers.abstract: Cao et al. [Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)] compared box-counting fractal dimensions of interfaces from continuum (SOLA-VOF) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of zero-Atwood-number mixing driven by random velocity perturbations. They reported D ~ 1.1-1.4 across physical models. We revisit their results with grid-converged geometric VOF simulations and modern box-counting algorithms. The grid-converged continuum dimension depends on the initial-condition realization (D = 1.13-1.38). Independent LAMMPS simulations show that Cao's MD dimension measures thermal scatter of atomic positions, not interface geometry, because their box-counting window lies below the scale of the interface structure: a flat interface at t=0 gives the same D ~ 1.36. When the thermal scatter is filtered by reducing the midpoint cloud to a curve (median binning at 2 sigma), the MD trajectory converges to the same late-time D ~ 1.43 as the continuum, recovering cross-model universality. We prove that the linear-regime box-counting dimension is exactly D = 2 - beta (A > 0) and D = 5/2 - beta (A = 0), where beta is the spectral exponent of the initial perturbation. For white noise (beta = 0) neither formula applies; Cao's early-time D ~ 2 is a boundary artifact. A three-dimensional grid convergence study gives D_3D = 2.361 +/- 0.002 at 400x400x200. Marstrand's co-dimension rule D_3D = D_2D + 1 shows a 7% discrepancy reflecting IC-realization dependence at A = 0, unlike the buoyancy-driven case where the discrepancy falls with resolution.

papers.title: Global Recovery from Local Data: Interior Nudging for 2D Navier-Stokes equations in a Physical Domain
papers.abstract: In many real-world applications of data assimilation (DA), the strategic placement of observers is crucial for effective and efficient forecasting. Motivated by practical constraints in sensor deployment, we show that global recovery of the flow field can be achieved using observations available only in a subregion of the domain, possibly far from the boundary. We focus on the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations posed in a bounded physical domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Building on the continuous data assimilation framework of Azouani, Olson, and Titi (2014), we rigorously prove that the assimilated solution converges globally to the true solution under suitable conditions on the nudging parameter, spatial resolution, and the geometry of the observation region, specifically, when the maximum distance from any point in the domain to the observational subregion is bounded by a constant multiple of \( \nu^{1/2} \) (in terms of scaling). Our computational results, conducted via finite element methods over complex geometries, support the theoretical findings and reveal even greater robustness in practice. Specifically, synchronization with the true solution is achieved even when the observational subregion lies farther from the rest of the domain than the theoretical threshold permits. Across all three tested scenarios, the local nudging algorithm performs comparably to full-domain assimilation, reaching global accuracy up to machine precision. Interestingly, observational data near the boundary are found to be largely uninformative. This demonstrates that full observability is not necessary: carefully chosen interior observations, even far from the boundary, can suffice.

papers.title: From Redundancy to Minimality: Fixed-Point-Guided Hierarchical Reduction of Learned Piecewise-Linear Dynamics
papers.abstract: Understanding a nonlinear dynamical system from time series requires not only reproducing its trajectories, but also identifying a simple representation that preserves its essential dynamical structure. Almost-linear recurrent neural networks (AL-RNNs) are piecewise-linear RNNs in which only a subset of units use ReLU nonlinearities, so that nonlinear capacity is explicitly controlled by the number of ReLU units. Their activation patterns define linear regions, represented as symbols, whose observed transitions form a symbolic transition graph. However, directly training AL-RNNs with few ReLU units to realize minimal dynamical representations can be unreliable. We ask whether an AL-RNN with more ReLU units can instead be trained first and systematically reduced to a minimal dynamical representation. We introduce a fixed-point-guided hierarchical reduction procedure that progressively linearizes selected ReLU units, merging neighboring linear regions and graph nodes while preserving distinct symbols containing fixed points (FPs). The resulting reduction tree defines a hierarchy of progressively simpler candidates. Each reduced candidate is initialized from the parent parameters and retrained through gradual linearization with guidance from the parent dynamics. We also prove that, under certain assumptions, reproducing $Q$ distinct fixed points requires at least $Q$ FP-containing symbols, providing a certificate of symbol-level minimality when this bound is attained. Across six tasks spanning attractor reconstruction and flip-flop memory, our learn-reduce-retrain strategy substantially improves the recovery of minimal models, including settings where direct training rarely succeeds. These results show that redundant nonlinear capacity can serve as a scaffold for discovering and realizing minimal dynamical representations.

papers.title: Learn Locally, Extend Globally: Koopman Eigenfunctions and the Basin of Attraction
papers.abstract: Koopman eigenfunctions associated with the Jacobian eigenvalues of a stable equilibrium are Lyapunov functions defined exactly on its basin of attraction. We turn this into a computational procedure for power systems. Eigenfunctions estimated by extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) are written as functions of the state, made to vanish at the equilibrium by centering the lifted variable $\cos\delta$, and verified on a grid with the model: two Lyapunov candidates from the EDMD spectrum certify up to 66\% of the basin of a single-machine infinite-bus system from data in the linear region. The Koopman semigroup property then extends the EDMD-Lie eigenfunction to the whole basin, recovered at the grid resolution with its isostables and isochrons.

papers.title: Existence of the C-type renormalisation two-cycle
papers.abstract: We prove the existence of the C-type renormalisation two-cycle, helping to establish the universality of the C-type route to chaos in families of non-invertible maps of the plane. Families of two-dimensional non-invertible maps, with at least two parameters and critical points of fold type, exhibit a distinct type of critical scaling, the C-type. An accumulation of parameter values leads to an infinite collection of coexisting attracting cycles of periods $4^n$ or $2\cdot 4^n$. Asymptotically, period quadrupling is accompanied by parameter-space scaling and state-space scaling governed by particular universal constants. Kuznetsov et. al. explained this phenomenon in terms of a stationary orbit of period two of the renormalisation group (RG) transformation for period-doubling. We prove the existence of the corresponding renormalisation two-cycle in a Banach space of analytic maps and gain rigorous bounds on the corresponding universal state space scaling constants. This result provides a further step in proving a series of outstanding conjectures concerning distinct universality classes for period-doubling. It extends the recent results for unidirectionally-coupled maps (the FS-type) to bidirectionally-coupled maps, and generalises the framework from fixed points to periodic orbits of the corresponding renormalisation operators. It also provides a further step in establishing the conjectured picture that the C-type universality class is born from the FS-type class via a period-doubling bifurcation in the dynamics of the RG transformation itself. The proof relies on rigorous computations to establish that a variant of Newton's method for the two-cycle is a contraction map. The C-type scaling regularity is known to occur in a number of dynamical systems of interest, perhaps most notably in biologically-plausible models of nephron blood pressure autoregulation.

papers.title: Effect of Colored Noise on Coupled Thermoacoustic Oscillators
papers.abstract: Noise can significantly influence thermoacoustic dynamics, yet the role of noise color in coupled thermoacoustic oscillators remains largely unexplored. Here, we examine the influence of colored noise on the dynamics of coupled thermoacoustic systems. The system consists of two coupled Rijke tube oscillators with time-delay and dissipative coupling. Stochastic forcing is modeled as an additive Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, such that white and colored noise contain equal power within a band around the system's natural frequency. We find that noise influences the system most prominently near the transition between limit-cycle oscillations (LCO) and amplitude death (AD) states, where increasing noise amplitude smoothen the transition and reduces the extent of the AD regions. Our analysis reveals the emergence of coherence resonance near instability threshold under both white and colored noise. The peak coherence factor varies with the noise color, with the largest peak coherence observed for colored noise whose correlation time is much shorter than the acoustic time scale. White noise and the shortest-correlated OU noise exert the strongest influence on both the pressure amplitude response and the coherence resonance. Overall, our results show that, under both coupling mechanisms, colored noise induces qualitatively similar trends in the system response, governed by its amplitude and correlation time.

papers.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
papers.abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. Near a stretch of 1/12 the saddle flapper resonates with the breathing of the ring. Below that stretch the flapper slows as it grows and above it the flapper speeds up, and near the resonance two families of saddle flappers overlap. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.
